{{Short description|Generalized natural number}}
[[File:Steinitz numbers svg.svg|thumb|400px|[[Hasse diagram]] of the [[lattice (order)|lattice]] of supernatural numbers; primes other than 2 and 3 are omitted for simplicity.]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''supernatural numbers''', sometimes called '''generalized natural numbers''' or '''Steinitz numbers''', are a generalization of the [[natural number]]s. They were used by [[Ernst Steinitz]]<ref>{{cite journal |last=Steinitz |first=Ernst |authorlink=Ernst Steinitz |date=1910 |language=German |title=Algebraische Theorie der Körper |journal=Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik |jfm=41.0445.03 |issn=0075-4102 |volume=137 |pages=167–309 |doi=10.1515/crll.1910.137.167 |url=http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?GDZPPN002167042|url-access=subscription }}</ref>{{rp|249-251}} in 1910 as a part of his work on [[Field theory (mathematics)|field theory]].

A supernatural number <math>\omega</math> is a [[Formal calculation|formal]] [[Product (mathematics)|product]]:

<math display="block">\omega = \prod_p p^{n_p},</math>

where <math>p</math> runs over all [[prime number]]s, and each <math>n_p</math> is either zero, a natural number or [[infinity]]. This can be thought of as the [[prime factorization]] of the supernatural number. In the special case where only finitely many values <math>n_p</math> are nonzero and no index <math>n_p</math> is <math>\infty</math>, we get the positive natural numbers; for example, <math>60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5</math> can be represented as
<math display = "block"> 2^2 3^1 5^1 7^0 11^0 13^0\dots</math>
There are also many supernatural numbers with no natural counterpart, such as
<math display = "block">2^1 3^1 5^1 7^1 11^1 13^1\dots</math>
and 
<math display = "block"> 2^1 3^\infty 5^0 7^0 11^0 13^0\dots</math>

Sometimes the notation <math>v_p(\omega)</math> is used instead of <math>n_p</math>. <math>v_p(\omega)</math> can be seen as the [[p-adic valuation]] of <math>\omega</math>, and it agrees with the standard p-adic valuation on the natural numbers.

There is no natural way to add supernatural numbers, but they can be multiplied, with <math>\prod_p p^{n_p}\cdot\prod_p p^{m_p}=\prod_p p^{n_p+m_p}</math>. Similarly, the notion of divisibility extends to the supernaturals with <math>\omega_1\mid\omega_2</math> if <math>v_p(\omega_1)\leq v_p(\omega_2)</math> for all <math>p</math>. The notion of the [[least common multiple]] and [[greatest common divisor]] can also be generalized for supernatural numbers, by defining

<math display="block">\displaystyle \operatorname{lcm}(\{\omega_i\}) \displaystyle =\prod_p p^{\sup(v_p(\omega_i))}</math>

and

<math display="block">\displaystyle \operatorname{gcd}(\{\omega_i\}) \displaystyle =\prod_p p^{\inf(v_p(\omega_i))}</math>.

With these definitions, the gcd or lcm of infinitely many natural numbers (or supernatural numbers) is a supernatural number.

Supernatural numbers are used to define orders and indices of [[profinite group]]s and subgroups, in which case many of the theorems from [[finite group theory]] carry over exactly. They are used to encode the [[algebraic extension]]s of a [[finite field]].<ref>Brawley & Schnibben (1989) pp.25-26</ref>

Supernatural numbers also arise in the classification of [[uniformly hyperfinite algebra]]s.
